review_note: Keep the opening, RFC clauses, signal-code comparison and mixed-classroom argument. Remove narrator commentary and assumptions about the reader; retain the practical scope limits.

edits.before:
Everyone in this room has run that exchange thousands of times. Some of you
run it without a thought and couldn't state one rule it follows.
edits.after:
Some of you run that exchange without a thought and couldn't state one rule
it follows.
edits.reason: Do not invent a shared history for everyone in the room.

edits.before: Two things follow, and both matter on day one.
edits.reason: The two following paragraphs already explain the consequences; cut the repeated signposting formula.

edits.before:
So the rules are not unknowable. Researchers have been writing them down for
over fifty years. They were written for other researchers, in a register
nobody outside the field reads, and then everyone went on behaving as if the
rules were self-evident. This is the engineering scandal the course is named
for. The protocol has documentation. It was never shipped to the users.
edits.after:
Researchers have been writing these rules down for over fifty years, for
other researchers. The protocol has documentation. It was never shipped to
the users.
edits.reason: Keep the deadpan punchline; remove the explanation of why it is an engineering scandal and the sweeping claim about readership.

edits.before:
We read his abstract, not the paper, so this page does not list the six. The
move is what matters here, and you will use it every week: **if you cannot say
what would count as an instance, you cannot check any claim you make about
it.** That is the difference between a specification and an opinion.
edits.after:
We read his abstract, not the paper, so this page does not list the six.
**Before testing a claim about greetings, say what would count as a greeting.**
edits.reason: Keep the evidence limit and usable method; remove the announcement of its significance and the closing maxim.

edits.before:
Hold that against everything in the next section. The corridor handshake
carries no information and is not a real question. That is a fact about **this
protocol**, in this kind of setting, and not a fact about greeting. Somewhere
else, the same slot in the same sequence is used to ask something and to get an
answer. The majority's version is a local implementation, and it is the one
this building runs.
edits.after:
The next section specifies **one local convention**: the handshake between
acquaintances passing in a corridor. Elsewhere, the same place in an exchange
can be used to ask a question and get an answer.
edits.reason: State the scope once, without turning a local working example into a universal claim about the building.

edits.before:
The branch is sometimes worth taking. The course's position is that you
should be able to see it while you're standing at the fork.
edits.after:
The branch is sometimes worth taking. Learn to see the fork while you're
standing at it.
edits.reason: Preserve the image and the choice; remove the announcement of the course's position.

edits.before:
Everything above assumes something the course has not yet earned: that the
opening **obliges** you to respond. Schegloff has a term in the
neighbourhood --- *conditional relevance* --- but this course only read his
abstract, so it will not define his term for you.
edits.after:
Why does an opening make a reply **expected**? Schegloff names *conditional
relevance*, but we read only his abstract, so we will not define the term
from that source.
edits.reason: Ask the substantive question directly while retaining the evidence boundary.

edits.before:
**If replies are hard for you**, notice that you have been treating every
opening as maximum obligation. Some are. Many are turned down low: a nod
answers a nod, and a person already walking away has mobilised almost nothing.
You are allowed to match the level you were given.
edits.after:
**If replies are hard for you**, you can match the level you were given. A
nod can answer a nod; a person already walking away may not be inviting a
conversation.
edits.reason: Avoid telling readers what they have been doing or feeling; give the practical option.

edits.before:
Then swap, and each name **what you changed** --- not how it felt. Position,
wording, timing, body. That list is the week's real artefact, and it is the
thing week 4 measures in milliseconds.
edits.after:
Then swap, and each name **what you changed** --- not how it felt. Position,
wording, timing, body. Keep the list for week 4's work on timing.
edits.reason: Retain the activity and useful cross-reference; remove the claim that this is the week's real artefact.

edits.before:
It is obvious to you
because you've run it ten thousand times, not because it is simple.
edits.after:
Familiarity can make the rules
hard to see.
edits.reason: Remove an invented count and a second polished contrast after the reader has already seen the mechanism.

edits.before:
Every week ends with lines you can check yourself against, and this one ends
below.
edits.reason: The self-check component immediately follows; the prose does not need to announce its own ending.
